title: Drennan v. Star Paving Co.
lead: A general contractor commits to a school bid using a paving quotation, and the subcontractor tries to withdraw for mistake before acceptance is communicated.

actors.name: William A. Drennan
actors.role: General contractor bidding on the Monte Vista school project.

actors.name: Star Paving Company
actors.role: Subcontractor submitting and then refusing the paving quotation.

proceedings: The trial court found a definite bid and reasonable reliance and awarded the replacement-cost difference.
Star appealed on revocation, mistake, and pleading grounds.
The California Supreme Court affirmed $3,817 plus costs.
limits: Use of the bid did not itself form a bilateral subcontract or purchase an option. The judgment awards damages rather than compelled paving, and does not decide an independent negligence theory.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Drennan receives last-day quotations for a bonded school bid
sections.cue: How did Star’s definite price enter his commitment?
paragraphs: On July 28, 1955, licensed general contractor William Drennan prepared a bid for the Monte Vista school in the Lancaster school district, due before 8 p.m. Local practice involved telephone subcontract bids on the same day. His secretary received about fifty to seventy-five, recorded them, and supplied them for his master cost sheet.

Late that afternoon Star Paving’s estimator quoted $7,131.60 for paving to the plans and specifications, repeating the number at the secretary’s request. Drennan listened on an extension, entered the amount, and used it as the lowest paving quote in his $317,385 total. He named Star as the paving subcontractor. Requirements demanded identification of subcontractors performing at least one-half of one percent of the work and a ten-percent bid bond. Drennan submitted the lowest general bid and received the principal contract.

sections.title: Star announces a mistake before Drennan can communicate acceptance
sections.cue: Why did the later search for another paver occur?
paragraphs: The following morning Drennan visited Star’s office. Before he communicated acceptance, its construction engineer said the bid was mistaken and Star would require at least $15,000. Drennan answered that he had relied on its quote, was committed to the school contract, and expected performance at that amount. Star refused.

Drennan sought replacement quotations for several months and eventually hired L & H Paving for $10,948.60, the lowest substitute bid he obtained. His later shopping followed Star’s refusal and sought to limit the loss; it did not precede his prompt insistence that Star honor its original quotation.

sections.title: Drennan recovers the difference and Star identifies the formation gap
sections.cue: What conventional theories did Traynor reject?
paragraphs: Drennan sued for the additional paving expense. The trial court found a definite offer to perform specified work at $7,131.60, reliance in preparing and submitting the general bid, and reasonable substitute cost. It awarded $3,817 plus costs. Star appealed, arguing revocation before acceptance, lack of option consideration, mistake, and insufficient damages pleading.

Justice Traynor accepted that no bargained-for option or already formed bilateral subcontract supplied the answer. Star had not requested use of its bid as consideration for keeping the offer open. Drennan’s use likewise had not bound him to award Star the work. The court therefore needed to explain why an unaccepted offer could nevertheless become temporarily irrevocable.

sections.title: Foreseeable reliance supports an implied commitment to leave the offer open
sections.cue: How did section 90 protect a later opportunity to accept?
paragraphs: Under the First Restatement’s § 90, a foreseeable and reasonable prejudicial change of position supported an implied subsidiary promise against revocation. Star quoted to obtain the subcontract and could expect a low figure to enter the general bid, help secure the principal award, and advance its own prospects. Drennan then became bound to the owner at a price calculated from that figure. Allocating the resulting risk to the bidder inducing the commitment protected a reasonable opportunity to accept after award.

Traynor compared § 45, which protects an offeree who begins performance invited by a unilateral offer through an implied promise not to revoke during completion. Foreseeable preacceptance reliance could justify similar protection where the offer contemplated a bilateral agreement. The comparison did not turn calculation of the general bid into performance Star had requested.

Protection was limited. A general contractor could not defer acceptance after award to seek a better price or reopen negotiations while keeping the original offer available. Drennan promptly expected performance; his subsequent replacement search mitigated an already refused bargain. An offer clearly reserving revocation before acceptance would be treated according to that reservation.

sources.pinpoint: Rule and Holding; Reasoning; Notes; 51 Cal. 2d at 413–17

sections.title: Star’s undisclosed mistake does not shift the committed contractor’s loss
sections.cue: Why was reliance on a low quotation reasonable here?
paragraphs: Drennan had no reason to know the figure was mistaken. Paving bids in the Lancaster desert region commonly differed widely; the court mentioned a 160-percent spread between the highest and lowest. A low quote alone therefore did not make reliance unreasonable.

Star’s rescission authorities involved known or reasonably apparent mistakes and an ability to restore the other party to its earlier position. Drennan had already undertaken the school contract. The court placed the loss with Star, which caused the mistake, rather than the contractor who reasonably committed on the quote.

The discussion of a possible negligence duty in preparing bids reinforced that allocation’s fairness, but the court expressly left open whether negligence alone would support a case tried on that theory. It did not find a separate negligence basis necessary to this recovery.

sections.title: Reasonable replacement efforts establish damages and the judgment is affirmed
sections.cue: What did the pleading objection and remedy actually decide?
paragraphs: Months of requesting bids and acceptance of the lowest substitute demonstrated reasonable mitigation. Drennan’s complaint alleged the amount paid for replacement paving. Any uncertainty should have been raised through a special demurrer, and Star’s failure to do so waived that objection.

On December 31, 1958, the California Supreme Court affirmed $3,817 plus costs. Chief Justice Gibson and Justices Shenk, Schauer, Spence, and McComb joined Traynor, with no separate opinion. Star was not ordered to do the paving.

The result separates reliance from both acceptance and consideration. Its precise recovery does not establish expectation damages for every promissory-estoppel claim. The later Second Restatement § 90 permits relief limited as justice requires, while § 87(2) more directly addresses offers inducing preacceptance reliance; those later formulations were not the text Traynor applied.
